During my undergraduate studies, my professor [Paulo Justiniano](http://leg.ufpr.br/~paulojus) always incentivized the students for using any Linux distribution on their machines. The reasons were vast, but I will give the details later on.

I never tried because I did not have a personal laptop at the beginning, and I was comfortable using Windows because I used this operational system on my internship and at home. On my last year of college, I had a personal laptop that came with Windows pre installed, and I was using as it is (knowing that migrating to Ubuntu would be better).

I remember like it was today. It was during the time that everyone was migrating from Windows 8.1 or 10. I was working on a report, had worked the full day on it, and then I decided to migrate to Windows 10. The migration run successfully, I opened the file, started typing a few more words, and then, out of nothing **my report became corrupted**, I could not save or send my report to anywhere, and I received the famous blue screen. I turned off and on my PC using the power button, but I could not see the original content of the file. It was gone. At the same time, I downloaded the Mint iso file, burn into a Pen Drive, and started using.

It was not only flowers at the beginning, as usual. My friend [Augusto]() helped my in the lab to install and do the basics. It has being passed some weeks, and I did not like the Mint, so I swap to Ubuntu. And then everything fell into place. All the troubles that I had when tried a fresh install on Mint it was solved on Ubuntu, and I could fix by my self. It really represents the meaning of Ubuntu: "I am what I am because of who we all are". Ever since then I use ubuntu on my personal laptop and in my current job. It is so amazing.

But I don't use Ubuntu just because I like; I use because it gives many advantages compared to Windows for me:

1. I know how to do a fresh install when needed.
2. It is free to use. Don't need to pay any license.
3. It hardly enters a virus
4. The performance does not go down over time
5. There is a full community open to help on askubuntu 
6. Due to the fact that most installation is made via CLI, it opens your mind to shell, to automate your repetitive tasks. 
7. It is portable.

When we talk specifically about Data Science tasks, I can list:

1. Python is pre-installed on Ubuntu 
2. Docker only runs on Ubuntu machines.
3. Almost every server in the world uses a distro based on Linux. Choosing a server on EC2, it is like to choose which Linux you want to use.
4. Installation of tools for data science such as R, Python, dependencies are usually easily handed on Ubuntu
5. A common task on a DS work is to tell the path you files are. If you are on Windows, you need to copy the path, paste on a Editor and invert the slash, or make it double. With Ubuntu, you do not. It is as is. 

The only thing that I miss on Ubuntu is the Office package. But using Libre Office is lighter, free and it is a good alternative full of customizations.

With all that given, I don't know why when someone starts a new job the infrastructure team never asks if the employee wants a Ubuntu/Windows to work. 

Leave in the comments any thoughts about it
